topics.label: Introduction and lecture framing
topics.groupedBecause: This opening frames the lecture as an integration of previously introduced immune cells and molecules.

topics.label: Principles of innate immune recognition
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how innate immunity distinguishes danger through molecular patterns and appropriately positioned, germline-encoded receptors.

topics.label: Toll-like receptor recognition and signalling
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how toll-like receptors translate microbial recognition into responses shaped by receptor location and cellular stress.

topics.label: Non-TLR recognition pathways and inflammasome activation
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics show how recognition pathways beyond toll-like receptors detect infection or damage and drive inflammation that can contribute to disease.

topics.label: Sentinel-cell activation and leukocyte recruitment
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics trace how activated sentinel cells initiate inflammatory responses that recruit circulating leukocytes to infected tissue.

topics.label: Lymphatic transport and adaptive immune priming
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explains how lymphatic drainage carries evidence of tissue infection to lymph nodes for adaptive immune activation.

topics.label: Excessive systemic inflammation and septic shock
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic examines how excessive inflammatory activation causes life-threatening systemic circulatory failure.

topics.label: Mechanisms of inflammation resolution
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explains how the balance between inflammatory stimulation and inhibitory signals brings an immune response to a stop.

topics.label: Tissue repair and persistent inflammation
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine why inflamed tissue may fail to return fully to normal, with persistent inflammation sometimes serving to contain an uncleared infection.

topics.label: Lecture close and next lecture
topics.groupedBecause: This closing ends the lecture and identifies complement as the subject of the next lecture.
